Why isn't there more variance in game pricing?

Because for some fucked up reason, developers feel (perhaps correctly) that if they don't price their game at the same level as other AAA games, consumers will presume the game is somehow inferior and won't buy it.

The same happened with UK universities when they raised the 'upper limit' for tuition fees a few years ago: everyone waited to see if Oxford and Cambridge would charge £9,000 (the limit), and then every other university in the country also charged £9000 so that potential students wouldn't presume their education would be inferior.

Actually, as a dude who has been into gaming now for 30+ years I'll tell you this is the best time for finding good value and deals in games.

In my day (gather round kids) there was no steam or gog, were no amazons or facebook trade groups, stores would rarely discount any games, even games that had been out for a long time unless they were total bargain bin shitware. You'd pay $50 for a NES game and it didn't matter if was a shit NES game movie tie-in or Super Mario 3. Solid PC titles never went on sale (everyone pirated them anyway, but still..) Now you wait 3-6 months and you find $60 games discounted down to $20-$40 all the time.

It seems that way if you only look at major AAA console or cross-platform releases. It's even more funny than that, because games in that price range get this "major AAA release" branding regardless of actual quality or content value.

You're asking two questions: why isn't there more variance and could some games generate more revenue if they launched at a lower price.

TL;DR: basic economic principles

More detailed reasons why the big games have a high initial selling price:

  • They are expensive to produce, and the distributors want to make money on their investment.
  • There is high demand...enough of us want the game when it comes out that we're willing to pay more. This is the same reason that new movies, iPhones, and other desirable products are not discounted.
  • There is a limited pool of potential buyers...gamers are a minority of the population, and even there, you have segments that only play certain types of games. Put this together with the preceding point and it's a good strategy to sell at full price to your loyal fan base early on.
  • People forget that the developers are not getting all of this money. The distributor gets a cut and the retailers (Gamestop, Amazon, Steam, MS Live, etc.) get a percentage of the selling price. If I were a developer of a game and dictated that my game could only be sold for $30, I might not get any of the players in the distribution channel to cooperate. If my discounted game is not available for people to buy, I go broke.
  • There is a secondary market in used games that developers don't really profit from. Again, it makes sense to maximize revenue early on before the used market erodes your revenue.

These reasons combine to set prices for new games at their current levels. And while in theory some company could try to achieve higher revenue by lowering up-front pricing, they take on additional risk against their high investment in producing the title.
